u435: His teacher stopped asking whether he had practised and instead asked what made practice hard. Joshua admitted it felt boring and he did not know how to practise. Together they made a ten-minute plan with one clear target per day, and he moved the keyboard next to his study table.
u436: Keep the keyboard uncovered and switched on near the study table
u437: Practise for ten minutes right after tea, before touching the phone
u438: Work on only four bars at a time, slowly
u439: Mark each practice day on a chart on the wall
u440: Record himself once a week to hear real progress
u441: The Bible honours skilful music. David was chosen partly because he was "cunning in playing" (1 Samuel 16:18), and the psalmist says, "Sing unto him a new song, play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psalm 33:3). Skill is not magic. It grows over time through faithful, small steps. Proverbs reminds us, "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Proverbs 22:29). Zechariah asks, "For who hath despised the day of small things?" (Zechariah 4:10). Ten minutes of slow scales may feel small, but God delights in growth that comes little by little. Joshua's practice can become worship, a way of offering his hands to God.
u442: God made the brain able to wrap repeated pathways in myelin, a coating that makes signals travel faster and smoother. This is why slow, focused repetition eventually makes playing feel easy. The process is designed to be gradual, so we learn patience and dependence. The boredom Joshua feels is often the feeling of new wiring being formed. God built us to grow by practice, not by instant download, so that skill comes with character. Every time Joshua practises, he is cooperating with the way God designed learning to work.
u443: Zechariah 4:10|For who hath despised the day of small things?
u447: Joshua practised on five days in the first week, then only twice the next week during exams. His teacher simply helped him restart. After three months he could play two worship songs smoothly and joined the youth team for one Sunday a month. He still finds scales dull, so he now plays one favourite song as a reward after them.
u448: Practice becomes possible when it is small, visible, easy to start and seen as growth rather than a test of talent.
u449: Joshua kept saying later, but later never came. When he played for just ten minutes every day, his fingers slowly got better.
u450: Ritika and the prayer that waited behind the reels
u451: Ritika, 26, a software tester in Bengaluru who loves Jesus
u452: Ritika gave her life to Jesus at a youth camp and still remembers how alive prayer felt then. Now she works long hours in an office. Each evening she comes home, eats, and tells herself she will spend thirty minutes with God before bed. First she opens her phone to reply to one message. Then one reel leads to another, then her friends start a funny group chat, then a show is releasing a new episode. Suddenly it is midnight. She whispers a tired prayer and falls asleep feeling guilty. On Sundays she sings with tears and promises God she will change. By Wednesday the pattern is back. She does not doubt that God is real, and she truly wants to know Him more. She simply cannot understand why something she values so much keeps losing to something she does not even enjoy that much.
u453: Research suggests that short videos are designed to deliver frequent, unpredictable small rewards, which strongly engage the dopamine system and make stopping hard. After a long workday, her prefrontal cortex, the part that helps with self-control, is tired. Prayer has no notifications, no novelty, and its rewards are deep but slower, so the brain undervalues it in the moment. Her intention is vague, so there is no clear cue for when and where to pray. The guilt after each failure makes prayer feel heavier, which adds to avoidance. Spiritually, Jesus described this exact tension: the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. Ritika's problem is not lack of love but a habit environment that works against her love.
u454: Ritika told a friend from church, expecting to be scolded. Instead her friend admitted the same struggle. They decided together that the phone would charge outside the bedroom, and that Ritika would pray right after dinner for ten minutes, before the phone came out.
u455: Charge the phone outside the bedroom from 9 pm
u456: Pray for ten minutes straight after dinner, in the same chair
u457: Keep a Bible and a small notebook on that chair
u458: Use an if-then plan, such as if I pick up the phone, I first read one psalm
u459: Message her friend each night with one word, done
u460: In the garden, Jesus found His disciples asleep and said, "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:41). He did not call them hopeless. He named their weakness with compassion. Paul admits, "For the good that I would I do not" (Romans 7:19). Ritika is in good company. Jesus Himself made space: "he went out into a mountain to pray" (Luke 6:12), and He often withdrew from crowds. The Lord calls, "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10). God is not angry at her late nights. He is inviting her into a rhythm where His presence is easier to reach than her phone.
u461: God designed our brains to respond strongly to reward, so that we would seek food, connection and joy. That same system can be captured by endless scrolling. He also gave us the ability to shape our surroundings and build habits, so that good choices can become easier over time. Because willpower runs low when we are tired, God's design invites us to plan ahead, use cues and lean on community. Prayer becomes easier when it has a set place and time, because the brain learns to expect it there.
u462: Matthew 26:41|the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak
u466: In the first month Ritika prayed on most evenings, though some nights she skipped it after outings with friends. She noticed she slept better without the phone in the bedroom. After two months the ten minutes often stretched to twenty because she wanted to stay. She still scrolls sometimes, but she no longer feels that her phone owns her evenings.
u467: When the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, we strengthen love for God by designing our evenings around Him.
u468: Ritika loved Jesus but her phone kept stealing her time. When she put the phone away and prayed at the same time each night, it became easier.
u469: Thomas and the Bible plan that turned to dust
u470: Thomas, 41, a schoolteacher and church elder in Kottayam
u471: Thomas has read through the Bible eleven times. Every January he begins a reading plan and ticks the boxes faithfully. But over the last two years the reading has become flat. He reads three chapters before breakfast, closes the Bible and cannot remember a single verse. Some days he skims Leviticus just to finish the box. He feels guilty because as an elder he is supposed to be an example. When young people ask him how to love the Word, he gives the right answers but feels like a fraud inside. He has started to dread his quiet time and sometimes skips it, then feels worse. He wonders whether something is wrong with his faith, or whether God has gone quiet. He still believes everything he reads. He just no longer enjoys it.
u472: Research suggests that motivation driven only by guilt or duty tends to be fragile, while motivation that comes from meaning and enjoyment lasts longer. Thomas's reading became about completing a task, so his brain began to treat it like any other chore. Rushing through large portions leaves little room for reflection, and the brain remembers what it thinks about deeply, not what it skims. Stress at school has also drained him. Spiritually, he has slipped from relationship into performance, partly from an old picture of God as a strict headmaster checking attendance. Dryness is also a normal season of faith that many believers pass through, not a sign of failure.
u473: During a retreat, a speaker asked everyone to read a single short psalm slowly three times and ask, what does this show me about God? Thomas cried over Psalm 23 for the first time in years. He realised he had been reading to finish, not to meet God.
u474: Read a short passage instead of three chapters
u475: Read it slowly two or three times
u476: Ask what it shows about God and what it invites him to do
u477: Write one sentence in a journal
u478: Turn the verse into a short prayer during the day
u479: The psalmist describes the blessed person: "his delight is in the law of the LORD, and in his law doth he meditate day and night" (Psalm 1:2). Jeremiah says, "Thy words were found, and I did eat them, and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart" (Jeremiah 15:16). Jesus warned religious people, "Ye search the scriptures... and ye will not come to me, that ye might have life" (John 5:39-40). The goal of Scripture is to meet Jesus. The Lord also says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good" (Psalm 34:8). Tasting is slow, not rushed. Thomas does not have to earn God's approval through his reading. He is invited to enjoy Him.
u480: God designed the brain to remember what it meditates on and connects to emotion. Slow, repeated reflection strengthens pathways and allows truth to move from the head to the heart. He also made us for relationship, so the brain is more motivated by love and meaning than by duty alone. Seasons of dryness are part of how faith matures, teaching us to seek God Himself rather than feelings. God built delight into us so that we would come to Him not only because we must, but because we want to.
u481: Psalm 1:2|his delight is in the law of the LORD
u485: Thomas changed his plan to one short passage a day. Some mornings still feel dry, and he has accepted that. But most weeks one verse lights up and stays with him. He now teaches the young people to read slowly and honestly. He still plans to read the whole Bible, but over two years instead of one.
u486: When Bible reading becomes dry duty, slowing down to meet God in a small portion can restore delight.
u487: Thomas read lots of Bible but felt nothing. When he read a little bit slowly and talked to God about it, he started to love it again.
u488: Aditya and the planner full of beautiful plans
u489: Aditya, 32, a marketing executive in Hyderabad
u490: Aditya loves plans. He has three planners, a productivity app and colourful charts for fitness, Bible reading, learning French and starting a side business. Every Sunday night he feels inspired and writes a perfect week. By Tuesday, the plan has fallen apart. He forgets meetings, starts five tasks at once, loses his keys twice a week and misses bill payments. He can work brilliantly when a deadline is close or a project excites him, sometimes forgetting to eat for hours. But ordinary tasks feel impossible to begin, even when he wants to do them. His wife is frustrated, and he feels deeply ashamed. He has watched every motivational video. Motivation is never the problem. He has buckets of it. He simply cannot turn it into action, and he has always been like this, since school.
u491: Research suggests there is a gap between intention and action, and plans often fail without specific cues. But Aditya's pattern goes further. His difficulty starting, losing things, poor time sense and bursts of intense focus have been present since childhood and affect work, home and faith. These can be signs of attention differences such as ADHD, where the brain's self-management and reward systems work differently. People with ADHD often need interest, urgency or novelty to get going. Shame builds when others call it laziness. This is educational, not a diagnosis, and only a qualified professional can assess it. Spiritually, he has wondered whether his struggles mean God is disappointed in him.
u492: After reading about attention differences, Aditya saw a psychiatrist and was assessed. He was diagnosed with ADHD. He grieved the years of feeling lazy, but also felt huge relief. With treatment and coaching, he learned systems that worked with his brain instead of against it.
u493: Seek a proper assessment when struggles affect every area of life
u494: Use one simple list, not three planners
u495: Break tasks into tiny first steps and set timers
u496: Work alongside someone, even on a video call
u497: Use alarms and visible reminders for bills and keys
u498: Treat himself with grace, not shame
u499: The psalmist declares, "I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalm 139:14). Aditya's brain is not a mistake. Paul writes that the body has many members, each different and needed (1 Corinthians 12:18-22). Paul also found that God's strength is shown in weakness: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Proverbs says, "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" (Proverbs 16:3). God does not shame Aditya for struggling. He invites him to seek wisdom, including medical help, and to rest in grace while he grows.
u500: God created great diversity in human minds. Some brains are drawn to novelty, creativity and quick bursts of energy, and these strengths can be wonderful. The same wiring can make routine tasks hard. God gave us doctors, research and community to help us understand our differences and find tools. Seeking help is not a lack of faith but wise stewardship of the body and mind He gave us. His design includes our need for one another, so that strengths and weaknesses are shared in the body of Christ.
u501: 2 Corinthians 12:9|My grace is sufficient for thee
u505: With treatment and new systems, Aditya now pays bills on time and keeps one daily list. He still forgets things and has messy weeks, especially when routines change. His wife learned about ADHD and became a partner rather than a critic. His prayer life improved when he began praying while walking, which suits his restless energy. He finally understands himself.
u506: When plans never turn into action across all of life, a kind assessment may reveal a brain that needs different tools, not more shame.
